precepts.text: Israel kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness, the Levites and the priests praising the Lord day by day. Passover is the destruction of Egypt and the deliverance of Israel, so every time we keep it we are rejoicing that God destroyed our enemies.
precepts.point: Rome, you just slaughtered a thousand Israelites, let me pray for you, is the stupidest thought there is, and it is the idea the black Christian holds and preaches.

precepts.text: A man defiled by a dead body or on a far journey may keep the Passover in the second month, the provision Hezekiah relied on.
precepts.point: They make a proclamation from Beersheba to Dan to come keep the Passover, for they had not done it for a long time in the way it was written.
precepts.why:
In the wilderness “they kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month at even”. But “there were certain men, who were defiled by the dead body of a man, that they could not keep the passover on that day”, and they asked, “wherefore are we kept back, that we may not offer an offering of the Lord in his appointed season”?

The Lord answered: “If any man of you or of your posterity shall be unclean by reason of a dead body, or be in a journey afar off, yet he shall keep the passover unto the Lord. The fourteenth day of the second month at even they shall keep it, and eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.” A man defiled or on a far journey may keep the Passover in the second month.

That is the provision Hezekiah relied on. Now that the temple was cleansed, the king and congregation took counsel “to keep the passover in the second month. For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem.” So he sent letters “to all Israel and Judah”, even “to Ephraim and Manasseh”, with a proclamation “from Beer–sheba even to Dan”, “for they had not done it of a long time in such sort as it was written.”

precepts.text: Speak the same thing, be of one mind and one judgment with no divisions, the same unity that gave Israel one heart to serve the Most High.
precepts.point: The great congregation removes the altars and incense altars in Jerusalem and casts them into the brook Kidron.
precepts.why:
“Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.” Speak the same thing, be of one mind and one judgment, with no divisions.

That is the same unity that gave Israel one heart to serve the Most High. “Also in Judah the hand of God was to give them one heart to do the commandment of the king and of the princes, by the word of the Lord.” And “there assembled at Jerusalem much people to keep the feast of unleavened bread in the second month, a very great congregation.”

Not everyone received it. The posts “passed from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh even unto Zebulun: but they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them”, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached. “Nevertheless divers of Asher and Manasseh and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came to Jerusalem.” And being of one mind, the congregation “took away the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for incense took they away, and cast them into the brook Kidron.”

precepts.text: Solomon and all Israel kept the feast seven days and seven days, even fourteen days, the earlier pattern Hezekiah's congregation repeated.
precepts.point: There is great joy in Jerusalem, for since the days of Solomon there had not been the like, and the priests and Levites bless the people and their prayer reaches heaven, his holy dwelling place.
precepts.why:
“And at that time Solomon held a feast, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt, before the Lord our God, seven days and seven days, even fourteen days.” That is the earlier pattern Hezekiah’s congregation repeated.

They “kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness”, and then “the whole assembly took counsel to keep other seven days: and they kept other seven days with gladness.” Fourteen days in all, all in one mind and one heart. Hezekiah gave “a thousand bullocks and seven thousand sheep”, the princes “a thousand bullocks and ten thousand sheep”, and all the congregation, the priests, the Levites and “the strangers that came out of the land of Israel” rejoiced together.

So it fits that “there was great joy in Jerusalem: for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was not the like in Jerusalem.” The priests and Levites blessed the people, “and their prayer came up to his holy dwelling place, even unto heaven.”

precepts.why: Some say there is to be no gladness on the solemn days of God, and make videos condemning those who rejoice, dance and drink on Passover. “And the children of Israel that were present at Jerusalem kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness”: great gladness, we were partying. “And the Levites and the priests praised the Lord day by day, singing with loud instruments unto the Lord.” We are supposed to play music and sing and dance and rejoice; God wants to see that, the beginning of a repentant heart. Nehemiah and Esther kept the feasts with gladness, even in captivity.

In Judah the hand of God gave them one heart to do the commandment. The sceptre and the lawgiver belong to Judah until Shiloh comes.

points: Many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover.
Hezekiah prayed, the good Lord pardon every one that prepareth his heart to seek God, though he be not cleansed. The Lord hearkened and healed the people, and this is the pattern behind Acts 10.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

points: Now that the temple is cleansed and the priests sanctified, Hezekiah sends letters to all Israel and Judah, even to Ephraim and Manasseh, calling them to keep the Passover at Jerusalem.
The king and congregation agree to keep it in the second month, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently and the people had not yet gathered in the first month.
They make a proclamation from Beersheba to Dan to come keep the Passover, for they had not done it for a long time in the way it was written.

The posts carry the letters through all Israel and Judah with the king's charge: turn again unto the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant escaped from the kings of Assyria.
Do not be like your fathers who trespassed and were given up to desolation, and do not be stiffnecked, but yield to the Lord and enter his sanctuary so his fierce wrath may turn away.

If they turn again, their captive brethren and children will find compassion and return to the land, for the Lord is gracious and merciful and will not turn his face away from those who return to him.
The posts pass from city to city through Ephraim and Manasseh to Zebulun, but the people laugh them to scorn and mock them, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached.
Nevertheless some of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humble themselves and come to Jerusalem, and in Judah the hand of God gives them one heart to do the commandment of the king.
The great congregation removes the altars and incense altars in Jerusalem and casts them into the brook Kidron.
They kill the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month, and the priests and Levites, ashamed, sanctify themselves and bring the burnt offerings into the house of the Lord.
Because many in the congregation were not sanctified, the Levites take charge of killing the Passover for everyone not clean.

Many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun eat the Passover otherwise than it was written, but Hezekiah prays that the good Lord pardon everyone who prepares his heart to seek God, and the Lord hearkens and heals the people. Grace and mercy are present here in the Old Testament.
The children of Israel keep the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness, then take counsel and keep another seven days, fourteen days in all, all in one mind and one heart.
Hezekiah and the princes give thousands of bullocks and sheep, and all the congregation, the priests, the Levites, and the strangers out of Israel rejoice together.
There is great joy in Jerusalem, for since the days of Solomon there had not been the like, and the priests and Levites bless the people and their prayer reaches heaven, his holy dwelling place.
